# Neural Audio Codecs {#sec-codecs}

@sec-codec-lm treated the token grid $\mathbf{C} \in \{1..V\}^{T_c \times N_q}$ as
given. This chapter opens the box.

A **neural audio codec** is a learned compressor: an encoder that maps a
waveform to a low-rate latent sequence, a quantiser that maps each latent frame
to one or more discrete indices, and a decoder that reconstructs the waveform
from those indices. It is trained end-to-end, usually with adversarial
supervision, and it plays two quite different roles depending on who is using
it. To a communications engineer it is a codec in the classical sense — a way to
transmit speech at 1.5 kbps instead of 256 kbps. To someone building a speech
language model it is a **tokeniser**: the thing that turns a continuous signal
into a sequence of integers so that the machinery of language modelling applies.

Those two roles pull in different directions, and much of what follows is about
that tension. A codec optimised purely for reconstruction produces tokens that
are hard to model; a codec optimised for modelling gives up fidelity. Nearly
every design decision in this chapter — frame rate, codebook count, semantic
distillation, quantiser structure — is a position on that trade-off.

::: {.callout-note}
## Reading order

This chapter assumes @sec-tts (which motivates codecs) and @sec-discrete-units
(which supplies the semantic-token half of the story). It is a prerequisite for
the speech language models of @sec-slm. Readers who want the
image-domain background will find VQ-VAE and VQGAN familiar
[@vandenoord2017vqvae; @esser2021vqgan]; this chapter re-derives what it needs.
:::


## Why Audio Needs a Tokeniser {#sec-codec-why}

The motivating problem is a rate mismatch, and it is worth quantifying because
the numbers are what force the design.

One second of English speech is roughly three to four *text* tokens. The same
second at 24 kHz is 24,000 *samples*. If you tokenise audio at the sample level —
$\mu$-law companding to 256 levels, as WaveNet did (@sec-wavenet) — a language
model with a 2,048-token context window sees **128 milliseconds** of audio at
16 kHz, which is less than one word. No amount of training fixes a context
window that cannot hold a single word.

This is not a thought experiment. Volhejn's Kyutai explainer runs it directly:
a 151M-parameter GPT-2-scale Transformer trained on 1,000 hours of Libri-Light
with sample-level $\mu$-law tokens produces speech-like babbling in which no
word is intelligible, the voice drifts, and generation of ten seconds takes
about thirty minutes on an H100. The failure is not acoustic — locally the audio
sounds like speech — it is a failure of *coherence over time*, exactly as
predicted by the context-window arithmetic.

So we compress. If the encoder downsamples by a factor of $D$ and emits $N_q$
tokens per frame, the token rate is

$$
\text{tokens/s} = \underbrace{\frac{f_s}{D}}_{\text{frame rate } f_r} \times N_q,
\qquad
\text{bitrate } R = f_r \cdot N_q \cdot \log_2 V \; \text{bits/s}
$$ {#eq-bitrate}

where $V$ is the codebook size. @eq-bitrate is the budget every architecture in
this chapter negotiates with, so it is worth grounding in real numbers:

| Codec | $f_r$ | $N_q$ | $V$ | Bitrate |
|:------|------:|------:|----:|--------:|
| EnCodec 24 kHz | 75 Hz | 32 | 1024 | 24 kbps |
| DAC 44.1 kHz | 86 Hz | 9 | 1024 | 7.75 kbps |
| Mimi | 12.5 Hz | 8 | 2048 | 1.1 kbps |
| WavTokenizer | 40–75 Hz | 1 | 4096 | 0.48–0.9 kbps |

: Frame rate, codebook depth, and bitrate for representative codecs. {#tbl-codec-rates}

Two observations follow immediately, and they organise the rest of the chapter.
**Frame rate is the most valuable axis** for a language model, because it
reduces sequence length linearly — Mimi's 12.5 Hz is a sixfold advantage over
EnCodec's 75 Hz before any other consideration. And **$N_q$ is a liability
rather than an asset** for a language model, because a model emits one token at
a time and $N_q$ tokens per frame must be serialised somehow (@sec-serialisation).
Compression research wants high $N_q$; modelling research wants $N_q = 1$.


## From Autoencoders to VQ-VAE {#sec-vqvae}

The cleanest way into vector quantisation is to leave audio entirely, which is
the route the Kyutai explainer takes and which I follow here because the
intuition transfers exactly.

Train an ordinary autoencoder on images — say Fashion-MNIST — compressing each
image to a two-dimensional latent. Plotting the latent space shows it clusters
naturally by class without ever being told the classes. Now quantise: maintain a
list of cluster centres (a **codebook**) $\mathcal{E} = \{\mathbf{e}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{e}_V\}$,
assign each latent to its nearest centre,

$$
k = \arg\min_{v \in \{1..V\}} \big\| \mathbf{z} - \mathbf{e}_v \big\|_2,
\qquad
\mathbf{z}_q = \mathbf{e}_k
$$ {#eq-vq-lookup}

and hand $\mathbf{z}_q$ rather than $\mathbf{z}$ to the decoder. The
consequence is immediately visible in the reconstructions: two images whose
latents land in the same cell decode to *exactly* the same output. Quantisation
is lossy in a very concrete, inspectable way.

### The Straight-Through Estimator {#sec-ste}

@eq-vq-lookup contains an $\arg\min$, which has zero gradient almost everywhere.
Training would stop at the quantiser.

The fix, in Volhejn's memorable phrasing, is to *pretend the problem does not
exist*. Treat $\mathbf{z}_q$ as $\mathbf{z}$ displaced by a constant, and copy
the decoder's gradient past the quantiser unchanged:

$$
\mathbf{z}_q = \mathbf{z} + \operatorname{sg}\!\big[\mathbf{e}_k - \mathbf{z}\big],
\qquad
\frac{\partial \mathbf{z}_q}{\partial \mathbf{z}} := \mathbf{I}
$$ {#eq-ste}

where $\operatorname{sg}[\cdot]$ is the stop-gradient operator. The forward pass
is unchanged; the backward pass behaves as though quantisation never happened.
This is the **straight-through estimator**.

There is a price, and it is worth stating because it explains the next
ingredient. The encoder is updated as if its output went to the decoder
unquantised, so the gradient direction is wrong by roughly the quantisation
error. The approximation is good only when latents sit close to their assigned
centres — which gives us a reason to *make* them sit close.

### Commitment, Codebook Updates, and Dead Codes {#sec-vq-loss}

The full VQ-VAE objective [@vandenoord2017vqvae] has three terms:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{VQ}} =
\underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}}(\mathbf{x}, \hat{\mathbf{x}})}_{\text{reconstruction}}
+ \underbrace{\big\| \operatorname{sg}[\mathbf{z}] - \mathbf{e}_k \big\|_2^2}_{\text{codebook}}
+ \beta \underbrace{\big\| \mathbf{z} - \operatorname{sg}[\mathbf{e}_k] \big\|_2^2}_{\text{commitment}}
$$ {#eq-vqvae-loss}

The **codebook** term pulls each code toward the mean of the latents assigned to
it — gradient-descent $k$-means. The **commitment** term pulls the *encoder*
toward the codes, penalising latents that stray far from their centre; this is
precisely what keeps the straight-through approximation honest. The two terms
are mirror images distinguished only by where the stop-gradient sits.

The codebook term is often replaced by an **exponential moving average** update
[@razavi2019vqvae2], which is more stable and is what DAC, Mimi, and most modern
codecs use. With $n_v$ the count of latents assigned to code $v$ in a batch and
$\mathbf{m}_v$ their sum,

$$
N_v \leftarrow \mu N_v + (1-\mu) n_v,
\qquad
\mathbf{M}_v \leftarrow \mu \mathbf{M}_v + (1-\mu)\mathbf{m}_v,
\qquad
\mathbf{e}_v \leftarrow \frac{\mathbf{M}_v}{N_v}
$$ {#eq-ema}

with $\mu \approx 0.99$–$0.999$. Under an EMA update the codebook is no longer
trained by the loss at all, so only the commitment term in @eq-vqvae-loss
contributes to the generator gradient.

**Dead codes** are the characteristic pathology. A code that is never selected
receives no update — under gradient descent or EMA alike — and therefore can
never move to where the data is. It is stranded permanently. The standard remedy
is blunt and effective: if a code goes unused for some number of steps,
**reinitialise it** to a randomly chosen latent from the current batch. Volhejn
describes this as *teleporting* the centre, which is exactly right. Dead-code
reinitialisation appears in almost every production codec, usually with a
threshold of a few hundred to a few thousand steps of disuse.


## Residual Vector Quantisation {#sec-rvq}

A single codebook of size $V$ contributes $\log_2 V$ bits per frame. To get
20 bits you would need $2^{20} \approx 10^6$ entries, which is prohibitive in
memory and in nearest-neighbour search cost, and hopeless statistically since
most entries would rarely be selected.

**Residual vector quantisation** obtains the same expressiveness from a cascade
of small codebooks by quantising what the previous stage got wrong. Recall from
@sec-ste that the quantisation error $\mathbf{z} - \mathbf{e}_k$ is already
sitting there in the straight-through computation. Quantise *it*, with a second
codebook, and repeat:

$$
\mathbf{r}_0 = \mathbf{z}, \qquad
\mathbf{q}_n = Q_n(\mathbf{r}_{n-1}), \qquad
\mathbf{r}_n = \mathbf{r}_{n-1} - \mathbf{q}_n, \qquad
\hat{\mathbf{z}} = \sum_{n=1}^{N_q} \mathbf{q}_n
$$ {#eq-rvq}

where $Q_n$ is nearest-neighbour lookup in the $n$-th codebook. Two codebooks of
1,024 entries give $2^{20}$ effective combinations from 2,048 stored vectors.

```python
def rvq_quantize(z, codebooks):
    residual, codes = z, []
    for cb in codebooks:
        quantized, index = nearest_code(cb, residual)
        residual = residual - quantized
        codes.append(index)
    return codes            # one integer per level
```

Three properties matter downstream.

**The levels are ordered by importance.** Codebook 1 quantises the signal itself
and therefore carries the coarse structure; each subsequent codebook encodes a
progressively smaller correction. This is not a designed hierarchy but a
consequence of @eq-rvq, and it is what makes the semantic/acoustic split of
@sec-semantic-acoustic possible.

**Bitrate is truncatable at inference.** Decoding with the first $n < N_q$
codebooks yields a valid, lower-quality reconstruction at a lower bitrate, with
no retraining. This only works well if training prepared for it, which is what
**RVQ dropout** does: randomly truncate the number of levels used during
training so the decoder never learns to depend on all of them. SoundStream
introduced this as "quantizer dropout" and Mimi uses it; a codec trained without
it must be retrained for each operating point.

**The output is a two-dimensional grid**, $T_c \times N_q$, which is the problem
of @sec-serialisation.

RVQ predates neural codecs by decades — it is standard in classical vector
quantisation — and reached audio through SoundStream [@zeghidour2022soundstream].
The same idea reached image generation independently [@lee2022rqvae].


## Codebook Collapse and How to Avoid It {#sec-collapse}

Codebook collapse is the recurring failure of this chapter, and the reader has
met it twice already: @eq-diversity was wav2vec 2.0's answer to it, and
CosyVoice 2's move to scalar quantisation (@sec-cosyvoice) was another. It
deserves a proper treatment here because codecs are where it bites hardest.

The failure is that a small fraction of codes absorb most of the probability
mass while the rest go unused. Effective bitrate then falls below the nominal
$\log_2 V$ bits per level: you are paying for a 1,024-entry codebook and using
200 of them. Four families of fix are in current use.

**EMA plus dead-code reinitialisation** (@sec-vq-loss) is the baseline and is
nearly universal.

**Factorised and $L_2$-normalised codes**, introduced by DAC [@kumar2023dac],
are the most cited fix. The idea is to perform the codebook lookup in a
*low-dimensional* projected space (DAC uses 8 or 32 dimensions against a
1,024-dimensional latent) and to $L_2$-normalise both latents and codes so that
lookup becomes cosine similarity on a hypersphere. Both changes make the
nearest-neighbour geometry better conditioned and dramatically improve
utilisation. This is the single most transferable trick in codec engineering.

**Finite scalar quantisation** [@mentzer2024fsq] eliminates the problem
structurally rather than treating it. Project the latent to a low dimension $d$
(typically 3–8), then round each dimension independently to one of $L$ levels
after a bounding nonlinearity:

$$
\hat{z}_i = \operatorname{round}\!\big( \lfloor L/2 \rfloor \tanh(z_i) \big),
\qquad
\text{index} = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \hat{z}_i' \, L^{\,i-1},
\qquad V = L^d
$$ {#eq-fsq}

There is **no codebook** — the "codes" are the vertices of a fixed integer
lattice, every one of which is reachable by construction. No commitment loss, no
EMA, no dead-code reinitialisation, no auxiliary entropy term. Gradients use a
straight-through round. FSQ matches learned VQ at comparable vocabulary sizes
while removing an entire category of failure, which is why it has spread quickly
into speech systems.

**Single large codebook with careful engineering** is the fourth route.
BigCodec [@xin2024bigcodec] and WavTokenizer [@ji2025wavtokenizer] abandon RVQ
for one high-cardinality codebook, betting that the modelling simplification is
worth the engineering difficulty. X-Codec2, the tokeniser behind Llasa
[@ye2025llasa], reports roughly 99% utilisation of a 65,536-entry codebook at
50 Hz — evidence that the collapse problem is tractable even at extreme
vocabulary sizes given the right lookup geometry.

### Per-Layer Entropy as a Diagnostic {#sec-entropy}

Collapse is usually reported as a single utilisation percentage, which hides
where it happens. A more informative diagnostic is the **entropy of the code
distribution at each RVQ level**, $H_n = -\sum_v p_{n,v}\log_2 p_{n,v}$, compared
against the ceiling $\log_2 V$.

A recent study of tonal content in codecs [@mondal2026tonal] reports such
profiles and finds the deficit concentrated in the **upper** layers: DAC at
32 kbps falls below 7.0 bits (of a possible 10) for codebook indices above 24,
and EnCodec at 24 kbps is worse. The proposed explanation is a data argument
rather than an optimisation one — upper layers encode fine residual detail, and
the signals that generate rich fine residuals (sustained harmonic material:
bells, glockenspiel, piano) are under-represented in ordinary training corpora,
so the upper codebooks are starved of the very data that would populate them.
Rebalancing training toward such content raised reported active-entry usage from
about 74% to about 95%.

The same work gives a usefully crisp definition of a *content-dependent* codec
failure — one that aggregate metrics hide. **Tonal weakness** decomposes into
harmonic artefacts (spurious components near harmonics), decay truncation
(premature clipping of long amplitude envelopes, giving an unnatural staccato),
and pitch instability (wobble on nominally steady tones). The DAC and EnCodec
papers both acknowledge degradation on this material without offering a remedy.

::: {.callout-warning}
## How much weight to put on this

The tonal study is a limited-scale result and says so: 720 hours of training
audio on four GPUs, compared against public DAC checkpoints the authors estimate
used 10–50$\times$ more data, with a 22-listener panel and large-scale
replication left as future work. Take the *diagnostic* — per-layer entropy, and
the observation that content under-represented in training starves the upper
codebooks — rather than the specific model or its benchmark numbers.
:::


## Training Objectives {#sec-codec-losses}

A codec is trained with a composite objective that inherits almost entirely from
the GAN vocoders of @sec-hifigan. Nothing here is conceptually new; what is new
is the quantiser sitting in the middle.

**Multi-scale spectral reconstruction.** An $L_1$ distance between log-mel
spectrograms of reference and reconstruction, summed over several STFT window
sizes:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{spec}} = \sum_{i \in S}
\big\| \log \operatorname{Mel}_i(\mathbf{x}) - \log \operatorname{Mel}_i(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) \big\|_1,
\qquad S = \{32, 64, \ldots, 2048\}
$$ {#eq-mel-loss}

Multiple resolutions are used because a single STFT window fixes one point on
the time-frequency resolution trade-off, and a model optimised against it can
exploit the blind spot. Short windows see transients; long windows see harmonic
structure and long decays.

**Adversarial and feature-matching terms.** A bank of sub-discriminators
$\{D_k\}$ — multi-period on the raw waveform (@sec-hifigan) plus multi-scale or
multi-band STFT discriminators — trained with a hinge objective, alongside an
$L_1$ match between the discriminators' intermediate activations on real and
reconstructed audio:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{adv}} = \sum_{k} \mathbb{E}\big[\max(0,\, 1 - D_k(\hat{\mathbf{x}}))\big],
\qquad
\mathcal{L}_{\text{fm}} = \sum_{k}\sum_{l} \frac{1}{N_{k,l}}
\big\| D_k^{(l)}(\mathbf{x}) - D_k^{(l)}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) \big\|_1
$$ {#eq-codec-adv}

**Quantisation terms.** The commitment loss of @eq-vqvae-loss, summed over RVQ
levels.

The total is a weighted sum, and the weights are lopsided in a way worth
noticing:

$$
\mathcal{L} = \lambda_{\text{spec}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{spec}}
+ \lambda_{\text{fm}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{fm}}
+ \lambda_{\text{adv}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{adv}}
+ \lambda_{\text{commit}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{commit}}
$$ {#eq-codec-total}

with typical values $\lambda_{\text{spec}} = 15$, $\lambda_{\text{fm}} = 2$,
$\lambda_{\text{adv}} = 1$, $\lambda_{\text{commit}} = 0.25$. A common practical
detail is a warm-up of tens of thousands of steps on reconstruction losses alone
before the discriminators are switched on.

::: {.callout-note}
## A consequence worth remembering

Because @eq-codec-total optimises perceptual and adversarial criteria rather
than waveform distance, adversarially-trained codecs can post **negative
SI-SDR** while sounding excellent — DAC reports around $-1$ to $-2$ dB. This is
not a defect; it means the model reproduces perceptual structure without
aligning sample-by-sample. It also means SI-SDR is invalid for comparing codecs
with different optimisation objectives, and that mel distance and perceptual
scores such as ViSQOL should carry the comparison instead.
:::


## The Codec Landscape {#sec-codec-zoo}

| Codec | Year | Rate | $N_q$ | Distinguishing idea |
|:------|:-----|:-----|------:|:--------------------|
| **SoundStream** [@zeghidour2022soundstream] | 2021 | 24 kHz, 75 Hz | ≤24 | First RVQ audio codec; quantiser dropout for scalable bitrate |
| **EnCodec** [@defossez2023encodec] | 2022 | 24/48 kHz, 75 Hz | ≤32 | Open, widely adopted; multi-scale STFT discriminator; optional entropy coding |
| **DAC** [@kumar2023dac] | 2023 | 44.1 kHz, 86 Hz | 9 | Factorised + $L_2$-normalised codes fix utilisation; Snake activation; the quality baseline |
| **SpeechTokenizer** [@zhang2024speechtokenizer] | 2023 | 16 kHz, 50 Hz | 8 | Distils HuBERT into RVQ level 1: semantic first, acoustic after |
| **Mimi** [@defossez2024moshi] | 2024 | 24 kHz, **12.5 Hz** | 8 | Split RVQ, WavLM distillation, causal/streaming, Transformer in encoder and decoder |
| **SNAC** [@siuzdak2024snac] | 2024 | 24–44 kHz, multi | 3–4 | Quantisers at *different temporal resolutions* rather than all at one rate |
| **BigCodec** [@xin2024bigcodec] | 2024 | 16 kHz, 80 Hz | **1** | Single high-cardinality VQ at Mimi-comparable bitrate |
| **WavTokenizer** [@ji2025wavtokenizer] | 2024 | 24 kHz, 40–75 Hz | **1** | Extreme compression, 40–75 tokens/s, one codebook |

: Representative neural audio codecs. {#tbl-codec-zoo}

Reading the table chronologically shows two trends running in opposite
directions. Fidelity-oriented work (SoundStream → EnCodec → DAC) pushes sample
rate and $N_q$ *up*. Modelling-oriented work (SpeechTokenizer → Mimi →
BigCodec/WavTokenizer) pushes frame rate and $N_q$ *down*, accepting fidelity
loss in exchange for shorter sequences and a simpler prediction target. These
are different objectives, not competing answers to one objective, and papers
that benchmark across the two groups on reconstruction metrics alone are
comparing things that were not trying to do the same job.

SNAC deserves a note because it breaks an assumption everything else shares.
Standard RVQ applies every codebook at the same frame rate; SNAC applies
quantisers at *different* temporal resolutions, so coarse structure is coded
sparsely in time and fine structure densely. This is a hierarchy along time as
well as depth, and it is the codec behind Orpheus among others.


## Semantic and Acoustic Tokens {#sec-semantic-acoustic}

@sec-audiolm introduced the semantic/acoustic split as a modelling decision made
*outside* the codec, using two separate tokenisers. The dominant modern approach
folds it *inside*.

**Semantic distillation** adds a loss encouraging the first RVQ level's output
to predict the representations of a frozen self-supervised model (@sec-ssl) —
HuBERT for SpeechTokenizer, WavLM for Mimi. The effect is to make codebook 1
carry phonetic content while leaving speaker identity, prosody, and channel to
levels 2 and up. Mimi refines this with **split RVQ**: rather than distilling
into the first level of a single residual chain, it runs a separate
single-codebook semantic quantiser *in parallel* with an acoustic RVQ, so that
the semantic objective cannot degrade the acoustic reconstruction path.

The clearest demonstration of what semantic tokens contain is an experiment in
the Kyutai explainer, and it is worth reproducing conceptually because it makes
an abstract claim concrete. Take a language model trained over full Mimi tokens.
Now generate with the **semantic tokens held fixed** from a reference recording
(teacher-forced) while letting the model freely sample all acoustic tokens.
Sampling twice yields two outputs that **say the same words in completely
different voices**. The semantic stream determines *what* is said; the acoustic
stream determines *how*.

That separation is what makes the split useful, for three reasons developed
earlier: linguistic coherence over long spans (@sec-audiolm), decoupled data
requirements (@sec-audiolm, via SPEAR-TTS), and a natural place to inject
speaker identity. A fourth is practical — because the semantic token is
$1/N_q$ of the token budget, its share of the loss falls as $N_q$ grows, so
systems weight it heavily. Moshi uses a semantic loss factor of 100.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The trade-off in one sentence

Lowering $N_q$ raises the semantic token's share of the loss and makes the model
*more linguistic*, at the cost of acoustic fidelity — which is why 8-level and
12.5 Hz codecs became the norm for speech LLMs even though 32-level codecs
reconstruct better.
:::


## Serialising the Token Grid {#sec-serialisation}

Here is the problem this chapter has been deferring. RVQ emits $N_q$ tokens per
frame. A language model emits one token per step. Something has to flatten a
two-dimensional grid into a one-dimensional sequence, and the choice is
consequential.

| Pattern | Mechanism | Cost |
|:--------|:----------|:-----|
| **Flattening** | Emit all $N_q$ levels of frame $t$, then move to $t+1$. One sequence, $T_c \cdot N_q$ long | Multiplies sequence length by $N_q$, undoing much of the compression |
| **Parallel** | Predict all $N_q$ levels of a frame simultaneously from one hidden state | Sequence length $T_c$, but assumes conditional independence across levels within a frame |
| **Delay / interleaving** | Emit level $n$ offset by $n-1$ frames, so each step predicts a diagonal of the grid | Sequence length $T_c + N_q$; level $n$ can condition on level $n-1$ of the same frame |
| **Depth transformer** | Large temporal backbone per frame, small autoregressive transformer over the $N_q$ levels within it | Exact factorisation, no independence assumption; extra module and per-frame serial cost |
| **Multi-token prediction** | Separate output heads emit all levels at once, trained jointly | Fast; recovers some cross-level dependency through shared representation |

: Patterns for serialising an $N_q$-level token grid. {#tbl-serialisation}

The tension is a factorisation question. The exact joint is
$p(\mathbf{c}_t) = \prod_{n} p(c_{t,n} \mid c_{t,<n}, \mathbf{c}_{<t})$.
Flattening represents it exactly at maximum sequence-length cost; the parallel
pattern drops the within-frame dependency entirely, which is cheap but wrong
(the levels of an RVQ frame are strongly dependent by construction, since each
codes the residual of the previous); delay patterns and depth transformers are
the compromises.

The **delay pattern** was popularised by MusicGen [@copet2024musicgen], whose
figure comparing flattening, parallel, and delayed interleaving is the standard
reference diagram for this material. The **depth transformer** comes from the
RQ-Transformer [@lee2022rqvae] and reached speech through Moshi
[@defossez2024moshi], where a 7B temporal backbone predicts one frame's context
and a small depth transformer autoregresses over that frame's eight levels.
Sesame's CSM uses the same split with per-codebook linear heads, and VALL-E's
AR/NAR pair (@eq-valle) is yet another point in this space — autoregressive over
time for level 1, parallel over depth for the rest.

::: {.callout-note}
## No convention has emerged

As of 2026 there is no standard. Every major system picks differently, and the
schemes have grown more elaborate rather than converging. This is a reliable
signal that the community has not found the right abstraction — and it is a
strong argument for single-codebook codecs, which dissolve the problem instead
of solving it.
:::


## What Is Actually Inside the Tokens? {#sec-codec-inside}

The account above is tidy: level 1 is semantic, higher levels are acoustic,
identity and prosody live somewhere in the middle. How much of that survives
measurement?

A 2025 interpretability study [@sadok2025interpretability] tests it directly
across four codecs with contrasting designs — DAC (pure reconstruction),
SpeechTokenizer (HuBERT-distilled RVQ), Mimi (split RVQ), and BigCodec (single
large VQ) — by tokenising LibriSpeech `test-clean` and measuring co-occurrence
between codec tokens and HuBERT's 100 discrete units, plus $t$-SNE structure and
mutual information estimated by a contrastive log-ratio bound.

| Finding | Detail |
|:--------|:-------|
| No deterministic token mapping | Codec tokens do not map one-to-one onto phonetic units; the best single-token association for BigCodec is about 8%. Codes take meaning from context, like words in translation |
| Distillation works, as designed | SpeechTokenizer's level 1 aligns strongly with HuBERT units and shows clean $t$-SNE clusters by phonetic class; DAC's level 1 aligns best among its levels, degrading with depth |
| **Leakage persists** | SpeechTokenizer's *residual* levels also carry linguistic content; Mimi's split RVQ, designed to prevent exactly this, still shows substantial content in higher levels — plausibly because 12.5 Hz frames each span several phonetic units |
| Identity lives in the middle | Speaker identity is barely present in SpeechTokenizer level 1, strongly present at level 4, still present at level 8 |
| **Pitch is the hardest** | Pitch shows essentially no interpretable structure in the embedding space, and the lowest mutual information of the three attributes |

: Empirical findings on the content of codec tokens. {#tbl-codec-inside}

The conclusion is that content, identity, and pitch are **entangled in the
quantised latent space even in codecs explicitly designed for disentanglement**.
The semantic/acoustic story is a real and useful tendency, not a clean
factorisation.

This matters practically in both directions. It explains why speaker identity
leaks into "semantic" tokens and why voice conversion by naive token surgery
does not work cleanly. And it motivates the factorised codecs behind the fourth
generation of voice cloning in @sec-cloning — NaturalSpeech 3's FACodec
[@ju2024naturalspeech3] and Spark-TTS's BiCodec [@wang2025sparktts] — which
impose disentanglement through explicit supervision, gradient reversal, and
information bottlenecks rather than hoping it emerges from residual structure.
Source-disentangled codecs [@bie2024sdcodec] pursue the same goal with
domain-specific codebooks. The same paper offers a
post-hoc route: train a masked encoder-decoder that maps bidirectionally between
codec tokens and interpretable attributes (content, pitch, loudness, speaker),
which both explains the tokens and enables controlled editing — swapping the
speaker attribute performs voice conversion.

The pitch result is the one I would flag for a reader. Pitch is perceptually
salient, prosodically essential, and is the attribute a reconstruction objective
has least reason to represent explicitly, since it can be reproduced
implicitly. If you want prosodic control, do not expect the codec to hand it to
you.


## Evaluation {#sec-codec-eval}

Codecs suffer a version of the evaluation problem already seen in @sec-tts-eval,
with a specific twist: **reconstruction quality and downstream modelling utility
are different objectives, and they can be anti-correlated.**

**Reconstruction metrics** are the mature half. Mel distance ($L_1$ on log-mel),
ViSQOL [@chinen2020visqol] and PESQ for perceptual quality, STOI for
intelligibility, SI-SDR for waveform alignment (with the caveat above that it is
meaningless across differing objectives), and MUSHRA or P.808 listening tests.
Codebook entropy and utilisation measure how much of the nominal bitrate is
actually used.

**Downstream utility** is what a speech LLM builder needs and is far less
settled. Two benchmarks address it. **Codec-SUPERB** [@wu2024codecsuperb]
evaluates codecs by how well downstream models perform on resynthesised audio
across recognition, speaker, and content tasks. **DASB**
[@mousavi2024dasb] ranks discrete audio tokens across discriminative and
generative tasks, and reports the result this section is built around:
**semantic tokens generally outperform compression-optimised acoustic tokens on
downstream tasks, while continuous representations still outperform both.**

Two consequences worth stating plainly. A codec that wins on ViSQOL may lose as
a tokeniser, so reconstruction leaderboards do not rank tokenisers. And the
finding from the tonal study [@mondal2026tonal] that higher-fidelity codecs
yield embeddings correlating somewhat better with human judgement — while both
remain below purpose-built contrastive audio encoders — is a useful reminder
that "the codec's latent space" and "a good audio representation" are related
but not the same object.

Toolkits: **ESPnet-Codec** [@shi2024espnetcodec] provides training and
evaluation across codecs with a unified metric suite, and **FunCodec**
[@du2023funcodec] offers reproducible multi-rate models.


## Do We Need Discrete Tokens at All? {#sec-continuous-alt}

The entire chapter rests on a premise worth interrogating, especially since
@sec-continuous-ar already showed it is contestable in synthesis.

The case *for* discreteness is architectural rather than representational.
Discrete tokens let you reuse the language-modelling stack unchanged: categorical
cross-entropy, sampling with temperature and nucleus filtering, KV caching,
pretrained text-LLM weights, and preference optimisation. That is a large amount
of borrowed infrastructure, and it is the entire reason the paradigm exists.

The case *against* is that quantisation destroys information for no modelling
reason. DASB's finding that continuous representations beat discrete tokens on
downstream tasks is direct evidence. MELLE (@sec-continuous-ar) generates
continuous mel frames autoregressively and is *more* robust than its
discrete-token counterpart. And a growing line of work generates continuous
audio latents with a small diffusion or flow-matching head per step, keeping
autoregression over time while discarding quantisation.

The honest position is that discreteness is an engineering convenience whose
representational cost is real and whose necessity is unproven. It is the same
open question raised at the end of @sec-ssl-open, arriving from the generative
side.


## Open Problems {#sec-codec-open}

1. **The fidelity/modellability trade-off is unquantified.** Everyone knows
   lower frame rates make sequences easier to model and reconstructions worse.
   Nobody can predict where the optimum sits for a given downstream model and
   compute budget, and there is no theory relating the two.
2. **Disentanglement remains aspirational.** As @sec-codec-inside shows, even
   codecs built for it leak. Whether clean factorisation into content, speaker,
   prosody, and channel is achievable without heavy explicit supervision is open.
3. **Serialisation has no principled answer.** @tbl-serialisation is a list of
   engineering compromises, not a solution. Single-codebook codecs sidestep it,
   which may be the real lesson.
4. **Pitch and prosody are under-represented.** A reconstruction objective has
   no reason to encode them explicitly, and measurement confirms it does not.
5. **Content-dependent failure is under-studied.** Tonal material is one
   documented case [@mondal2026tonal]; the general question of which signal
   classes a codec systematically mishandles, and whether that is a data problem
   or a capacity problem, is largely unexplored. Aggregate metrics hide it by
   construction.
6. **Evaluation for tokenisers, not compressors.** Codec-SUPERB and DASB are
   starts, but there is no accepted way to predict how a codec will behave inside
   a speech LLM without training one.
7. **Streaming and latency constraints.** Causality, low algorithmic delay, and
   cheap decoding are required for duplex dialogue and constrain everything else;
   Mimi's sub-10 ms CPU decode is the target to beat.
8. **Non-speech audio and general audio.** Most speech codecs degrade on music
   and environmental sound. Whether one tokeniser should serve all audio, or
   whether domain-specific codecs are the right answer, is unsettled.


## Summary

A neural audio codec is an encoder, a quantiser, and a decoder, trained
end-to-end with spectral, adversarial, feature-matching, and commitment losses.
It exists because language models need discrete tokens at a manageable rate:
sample-level modelling puts less than one word inside a typical context window,
which is a failure of coherence no amount of training repairs.

The technical core is vector quantisation made trainable. The $\arg\min$ lookup
has no gradient, so the straight-through estimator copies the gradient past it;
the commitment loss keeps that approximation honest by pulling latents toward
their codes; EMA updates and dead-code reinitialisation keep the codebook alive.
Residual quantisation then buys exponential vocabulary from linear storage by
quantising each stage's error, which incidentally orders the levels by
importance and makes bitrate truncatable — and which produces the
two-dimensional token grid that every downstream language model must serialise,
with no consensus on how.

Codebook collapse is the recurring adversary, and the progression of fixes —
diversity losses, EMA and dead-code reinitialisation, factorised and normalised
lookup, and finally finite scalar quantisation, which removes the codebook
entirely — is the same movement toward structural rather than corrective
solutions seen in @sec-ssl-compare.

Two ideas deserve to be carried forward. The **semantic/acoustic split**, now
usually folded inside the codec by distilling a self-supervised model into the
first level, is what makes speech language modelling a linguistic rather than an
acoustic act; holding semantic tokens fixed while resampling the rest yields the
same words in a different voice, which is the cleanest demonstration available
of what these representations contain. And the **empirical caveat** to that
story: measurement shows content, identity, and pitch remain entangled even in
codecs designed to separate them, with pitch the least represented of all.

@sec-slm takes the token grid as an interface and asks what happens when a
language model is trained to read and write it — and why, so far, doing so makes
the language model worse at thinking.
